clue.text: Run into thicket to find evidence of murder?

indicators.note: into tells you the letter for a run goes inside the word for a thicket, not beside it

parts.note: a copse is a small thicket of trees
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone dashes into the undergrowth looking for proof that a killing took place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run into' reads as a verb of motion, but 'Run' is the cricket abbreviation R and 'into' places it inside COPSE. The question mark admits that a body is only one kind of such evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a dead body is the most obvious proof that a killing has happened, and the question mark marks it as only one possibility.

clue.text: Doctor saying when temperature's dropped a bit?

parts.note: MO is short for medical officer, a doctor in the armed forces

indicators.note: dropped tells you the letter for temperature falls out of the word for a saying

parts.note: a dictum is a formal saying or pronouncement
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature; the 's is short for 'has' and gives no letter

explanation.surface: A doctor remarks on the moment a patient's fever has come down slightly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a doctor talking about a fever, but 'saying' is a noun, and 'dropped' takes the abbreviation for temperature out of it to leave DICUM. 'when' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: each names a small amount of something, as in showing only a little common sense.

clue.text: Brown bits and pieces left abandoned

indicators.note: abandoned tells you the letter for left is given up by the word for household clutter

parts.note: in British English this word for sawn timber also means stored odds and ends, household junk

explanation.surface: Brown odds and ends lie where somebody dumped them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left abandoned' reads as one phrase about dumped junk, but 'left' is the abbreviation L and 'abandoned' removes it from LUMBER, which in British English means stored odds and ends as well as timber.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is an earth pigment and the dark yellowish shade of brown named after it.

clue.text: Reverberated as an alarm initially ignored?

definitions.meaning: the plain sense: rang out and echoed loudly
the playful sense: an alarm nobody heeded the first time goes off a second time, which a prefix meaning 'again' expresses

explanation.surface: A noise echoed around like an alarm that nobody paid attention to at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially ignored' looks like an order to drop a first letter, but nothing is removed. An alarm ignored at first (think of a snooze button) goes off again, so it RE-SOUNDED.
explanation.definitionFit: A noise that echoed rang out loudly, and an alarm unheeded at first has gone off a second time, which the prefix for again expresses.

clue.text: Does what many a road worker does to get a bit of food

parts.words: Does what many a road worker does
parts.note: the verb half of the phrase: a worker closing a lane lets each marker fall from the lorry onto the tarmac, in the third person to match 'Does'

parts.words: Does what many a road worker does
parts.note: the object half of the phrase: the orange plastic marker that road crews set out in rows, in the singular

explanation.surface: A labourer on the roads does his usual job in order to earn something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase about the road worker is a playful description: he DROPS a traffic CONE. Shift the word break one letter to the left for a small thick pancake, a teatime favourite in Scotland and northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a small thick pancake made by letting spoonfuls of batter fall onto a hot griddle, so one is a small item to eat.

clue.text: Carelessness not unknown in ministers? No

definitions.note: the question and its answer together mean people who are not ministers, a plural idea that one collective noun names

indicators.note: not tells you the word for carelessness goes without the letter that 'unknown' stands for

parts.note: laxity is slackness, a lack of proper care
X is the algebraic symbol for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: Asked whether sloppiness is ever found among the clergy, someone answers with a flat denial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not unknown' is an everyday understatement, but here 'not' removes X, the algebraic unknown, from LAXITY. The definition is the closing question with its answer, meaning people who are not clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by exclusion: the word names the ordinary members of a church, everyone who is not ordained clergy.

clue.text: Fashionable model enthrals men, but not yours truly

indicators.note: to enthral is to hold captive, so the word for a model holds what follows inside it

parts.note: a toy can be a miniature model, as in a toy soldier or toy train

indicators.note: but not tells you the letters for 'yours truly' are taken away from the word just before

parts.note: taken as written
'yours truly' is a jokey way of saying 'me'

explanation.surface: A stylish catwalk model captivates every man except the person speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'model' is not a catwalk figure but a TOY, which 'enthrals' (holds) N: that is 'men' once 'but not' has removed ME. Tony is a chiefly American word for stylish and upmarket.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a chiefly American informal adjective meaning stylish, upmarket and high-toned, as in a smart neighbourhood.

clue.text: Notice maiden asleep with husband in bed spoken ill of

indicators.note: in tells you the four short pieces lie between the letters of the word for a bed

parts.note: taken as written
an ad, short for advertisement, is a public notice
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden, an over in which no runs are scored
someone who is out, as in out like a light, is asleep or unconscious
H is the abbreviation for husband used in family trees

explanation.surface: Someone spots a young woman asleep in bed beside her husband, and she is the subject of nasty gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in bed' looks like where the couple are lying, but 'in' is a container signal: the four short pieces go inside BED itself. M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to criticise or disparage someone behind their back, here in the passive past participle to match the phrase.

clue.text: Successful rustler will have assessed the situation

definitions.meaning: the playful sense: a rustler steals cattle, so one who got away with it will have made off with the farmer's animals
the idiomatic sense: reviewed how things stand before deciding what to do

explanation.surface: A cattle thief who got away with it must have sized things up carefully beforehand.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence but splits after 'have': a rustler steals cattle, so a successful one will have TAKEN STOCK (livestock), which is also the idiom for having reviewed one's position.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler who succeeded has stolen cattle, the farmer's livestock, and the same idiom means having reviewed one's position before acting.

clue.text: Swear in wild party, beginning to end

indicators.note: beginning to end tells you the first letter of the word for a party travels round to the back

parts.note: a rave is a wild all-night dance party

explanation.surface: Someone curses all through a riotous party, from the moment it starts until it finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to end' looks like a span of time, but it sends the first letter of RAVE to the back. 'Swear' here means declare solemnly, not curse, and 'in' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to state something solemnly and positively as true, as a witness does under oath.

clue.text: Grotesque once opposing change at first

parts.note: anti means against, opposed to something

indicators.note: at first tells you to keep only the opening letter of the word just before it

explanation.surface: A bizarre character who in earlier days resisted reform to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' belongs to the definition: the adjective meaning grotesque is archaic, as in Hamlet's 'antic disposition'. 'at first' keeps only the opening letter of 'change'.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic synonym: as an adjective it formerly meant bizarre or fantastic, the sense in Hamlet's feigned madness, and 'once' flags the usage as obsolete.

clue.text: Originator of research into outbreak of disease affecting part of the skin

indicators.note: into tells you the single letter goes inside the word for an outbreak

parts.note: an epidemic is a widespread outbreak of an infectious disease

indicators.note: the originator of a word is the letter that starts it, so keep only the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: The scientist who began the study of a spreading infection that attacks an area of the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Originator of research' sounds like a pioneering scientist, but 'Originator of' asks only for the first letter of 'research', which 'into' places inside EPIDEMIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjective for adjectival phrase: it means relating to the epidermis, the thin outer layer of the skin.

clue.text: When some won't drink with one type of glass?

parts.note: Lent is the forty days before Easter, when many Christians give up alcohol or another pleasure
I is the Roman numeral for one
a form of something is a type or kind of it

explanation.surface: Someone wonders at what point certain people refuse a drink when handed one particular kind of glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type of glass' looks like one phrase for a tumbler or flute, but it splits: 'type' is FORM and only 'of glass' defines. The glass is a lens, so the answer means lens-shaped; 'with' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose sense flagged by the question mark: the adjective means shaped like a lens, and a lens is a piece of glass.

clue.text: Leader of orchestra appearing at the end of concert video?

indicators.note: appearing at the end of tells you the single letter is placed after the word for a concert, not before it

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as in the BBC Proms held in London each summer

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its head, so keep only the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: The principal violinist shows up in the closing moments of a film of the performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The leader of an orchestra is its principal violinist, but 'Leader of' wants only the first letter of 'orchestra', and 'appearing at the end of' sends it after PROM. The question mark shows the answer is just one kind of video.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a short promotional film, such as the clip made to advertise a pop single, so only one kind of video.

clue.text: Suggest schoolmaster has inner perception most don't have?

indicators.note: has inner tells you the word for a schoolmaster holds the next piece within itself

parts.note: beak is dated British slang for a schoolmaster, and also for a magistrate
ESP, extrasensory perception, is the sixth sense that few people claim to possess

explanation.surface: Hint that the teacher possesses an inward insight that the rest of us lack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inner perception' reads as one idea, but 'inner' belongs with 'has': 'has inner' makes the schoolmaster, in old British public-school slang, hold the sixth sense that most people lack.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both mean to be a sign of or point to something, as fine clothes point to wealth.

clue.text: Vessel's part in westbound journey retraced

indicators.note: westbound says the hidden letters are read backwards
part in tells you the answer forms a stretch of the letters of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A ship's role in a voyage towards the west that goes back over an earlier route.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Vessel' alone, a blood vessel and not a ship's component: 'part in' hides the answer inside 'journey retraced', and 'westbound' reads YRETRA right to left in this across entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a blood vessel, one of the tubes carrying blood away from the heart.

clue.text: What could be acted out with seizure of power

definitions.text: What could be acted out with seizure of power

indicators.note: with seizure of tells you the rearranged letters seize, that is take in, the letter for power
could be says the two words after it might turn into something else, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; these eight letters are the ones rearranged
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Something that might be staged dramatically when a group grabs control of a country.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay. 'could be' rearranges ACTED OUT into COUDETAT, and 'with seizure of' makes that take in P, the physics symbol for power.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes it: a sudden, often violent overthrow of a government, a drama staged by those grabbing control.

clue.text: Smooth drive round part of East End taking in docks initially

indicators.note: round tells you the word for a drive goes on the outside, wrapped about everything else

parts.note: a run is a short drive, as in a run out to the coast in the car

indicators.note: taking in tells you the district's name admits the single letter that follows

parts.note: Bow is a district in the East End of London

indicators.note: initially tells you to keep only the first letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: An easy car journey around a stretch of London's East End, with a look at the docks to start.
explanation.walkthrough: A box inside a box: 'round' wraps the drive about the London district, which by 'taking in' holds the letter that 'initially' picks. 'Smooth' is a verb here, not a description of the drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to sand or wipe a surface until it is even, as a decorator does to woodwork before painting.

clue.text: With their time coming to end, big shops may become most annoyed

indicators.note: coming to end tells you the letter for time travels to the back of the word for the shops

parts.note: stores are large shops, as in department stores

explanation.surface: As their era draws to a close, the large retailers could turn extremely irritated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time coming to end' sounds like the decline of the high street, but 'coming to end' moves T, the abbreviation for time, from second place in STORES to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the superlative: sore is informal, chiefly American, for angry or resentful, so the -est form means angriest.

clue.text: Stroke this person, fool taken in

indicators.note: taken in tells you the word for a fool is swallowed by the word for the speaker

parts.note: the setter calls himself 'this person', which in his own mouth is ME
an ass is a foolish person

explanation.surface: Caress this gullible individual, an idiot who has been thoroughly deceived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' is not a caress but a billiards shot, played with the cue held almost upright so the ball swerves. 'taken in' means swallowed, not deceived.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a billiards or snooker shot made with the cue nearly vertical, putting swerve on the ball.

clue.text: Share a room and respond to a very funny situation?

definitions.meaning: what two travellers do when a single bedroom has to serve for both of them

definitions.text: respond to a very funny situation
definitions.meaning: to bend over helplessly with laughter, the body folding at the waist

explanation.surface: Two friends take one hotel room and react to something hilarious.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions joined by 'and': squeezing two people into one bedroom, and folding over with helpless laughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are senses of one phrasal verb: two people squeezing into one bedroom, and a person bending over with helpless laughter.

clue.text: A theologian is held by church to be dishonourable

indicators.note: held by tells you the three pieces before it sit between the letters of the abbreviation for church

parts.note: taken as written
DD is Doctor of Divinity, the degree of a senior theologian
taken as written

explanation.surface: The church authorities judge a certain religious scholar to have behaved disgracefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface has the church passing judgement on a scholar, but 'held by' is physical containment and 'to be' only joins. The answer comes from cad, dated British slang for a man who behaves without honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: behaving like a cad, a dated British word for a man who treats others, especially women, without decency.

clue.text: Virile but heartless, duke bound to be in insane mode

indicators.note: bound means tied up or enclosed, so the letter for duke is held inside what remains of the first word
heartless tells you the word for virile loses its heart, the middle one of its five letters

parts.note: manly means virile, having qualities traditionally thought masculine
the middle letter of the five-letter word for virile, the heart that is removed

explanation.surface: A macho but cruel nobleman is certain to end up in a deranged state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' removes the middle letter of MANLY, leaving MALY, and 'bound' ties D for duke into the gap. Only in the surface does 'bound to be' mean certain to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Adverb for adverbial phrase: to act in an insane manner is to act wildly or crazily.

clue.text: Conceited in rank? Nothing good in that

indicators.note: in that tells you the two letters go inside 'that', the word for rank mentioned just before

parts.note: arrant and rank both mean utter or downright, as in arrant nonsense and rank stupidity
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone vain about their high position is told there is no merit in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rank' is not social standing but the adjective meaning utter, ARRANT; 'in that' puts O and G inside it, 'that' pointing back to the word for rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both describe someone with an exaggerated opinion of their own importance, proud and overbearing.

clue.text: Speed of sound's nothing, male admitted — that's his swaggering style

indicators.note: admitted tells you the letter for male is let into the run of letters built so far

parts.note: Mach 1 is the speed of sound, named after the physicist Ernst Mach, so his name stands for it here
the apostrophe-s is read as the short form of 'is'
O looks like zero, nothing
M is the abbreviation for male, as on forms

explanation.surface: A man concedes that breaking the sound barrier is trivial, which is typical of his boastful manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound's' hides a split: Mach is the measure of the speed of sound and the apostrophe-s is IS. 'admitted' is not confessed but let in, placing M before the final O.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: aggressive masculine pride, the strutting show of toughness that 'his' attributes to the male in the clue.

clue.text: Woman minister's residence in published list

parts.note: Di, short for Diana, is a woman's name that crosswords use often
a rectory is the house provided for a rector, a parish priest in the Church of England

explanation.surface: The home of a female member of the clergy appears in a printed register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman minister' reads as one person, a female priest, but the words must be split: 'Woman' alone is the name DI, and the residence is any minister's. 'in' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a book or file listing names with addresses or numbers, such as a telephone book.

clue.text: Island resident catching cold becomes lethargic

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for island, as on maps

indicators.note: catching tells you the word for a resident takes hold of the letter for cold inside it

parts.note: a native is someone born and living in a place, a local resident
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Someone living on an island comes down with a chill and turns sluggish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Island resident' looks like one person, an islander, but splits into I and NATIVE; 'catching cold' is not an illness but NATIVE taking in C, the letter on a cold tap.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both describe someone sluggish and idle, doing little or nothing.

clue.text: Chemicals providing essential colours from what we hear

indicators.note: from what we hear tells you the phrase for essential colours is to be listened to, not spelt

parts.note: key means essential, as in a key ingredient; tones are shades of colour

explanation.surface: Chemical compounds supply the vital pigments, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from what we hear' asks you to say the two-word phrase for essential colours aloud; run together, it sounds like a family of organic compounds of which acetone is the simplest.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: they are a class of organic compounds containing a carbonyl group, acetone being the simplest.

clue.text: Quickly leave head of valley pursued by a wild animal

indicators.note: pursued by tells you the letter from the valley comes first and the other pieces follow behind it
the head of a word is its top letter in a down entry, so keep only the first letter of the next word

parts.note: taken as written
a moose is a large wild deer of North America

explanation.surface: Get out of the top end of the valley fast, with a savage beast chasing you.
explanation.walkthrough: The head of a valley is a real place in the surface, but 'head of' takes only the first letter of 'valley', and 'pursued by' puts A and MOOSE after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: informal, from Spanish 'vamos' (let's go), meaning to depart in a hurry.

clue.text: Midlands town sets record in what's drunk in pub

indicators.note: in tells you the record goes inside the word for the pub drink; 'sets' is the verb that goes with it

parts.note: beer is the usual drink ordered in a pub
an LP is a long-playing vinyl record

explanation.surface: A town in the English Midlands achieves a new high for the amount drunk in its pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sets record' is not an achievement: 'sets' with 'in' places a vinyl album inside the pub drink. The answer is a market town in Derbyshire, in the English East Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: it is a market town in the Derwent valley in Derbyshire, in the East Midlands of England.

clue.text: A bid to be funny, line thrown in?

definitions.text: A bid to be funny, line thrown in

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: thrown in tells you the letter for line is tossed into the middle of the rearranged letters
funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters of the word before it are put in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written; these three letters are the ones rearranged
L is the abbreviation for line, as in references to a page of text

explanation.surface: An attempt at humour, with an extra remark tossed into the conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay. After A, 'to be funny' rearranges BID into DIB, and 'thrown in' drops L for line inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes it: an unscripted remark, often a joke, that a performer drops in on the spur of the moment.

clue.text: Modern publication upheld honour all right

indicators.note: upheld means held up, and in a down entry that turns the word for an honour to read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the OBE, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, is a British state honour
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A recently launched magazine has rightly defended somebody's good name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upheld' means defended in the surface, but in this down entry it turns OBE (a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire) upwards into EBO.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a text issued in digital form for reading on a screen, a product of recent decades.
